# LIMSOC Incident Categorisation

Operational Change Proposal, v0.8, 2 August 2026

*LIMSOC-BRIEF-LSV-2026-001 | Season 2026-27 | Focus Area 1: Enhance Our Incident Management | Working draft, not yet SME-circulated*

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| brief_id | LIMSOC-BRIEF-LSV-2026-001 |
| project_ref | 1.1 New Incident Categorisation |
| focus_area | 1. Enhance Our Incident Management |
| season | 2026-27 |
| status | draft v0.8 |
| owner | Nicholas Wood |
| sme_group | Incident Categorisation and Flow |
| themes | Simplification, Cohesion |
| last_updated | 2026-08-02 |

## About this pack

This pack proposes a new incident categorisation model for LIMSOC, Life Saving Victoria's operational incident-management system, and maps every current incident type to the new model. Nothing in this pack is endorsed yet.

**How to read it.** Part 1 explains the problem we have today. Part 2 explains the proposed model, one concept at a time, and why each piece exists. Part 3 describes what will change for operators, duty officers, and our leadership. Part 4 covers what happens next and what we need from you. The annexes hold the working detail: the full migration map for all 72 current types, the decision log, and the platform notes.

Feedback to Nicholas Wood, State Lifesaving Communications Officer.

---

# Part 1: The case for change

## The problem

Ask two experienced operators what an incident type means and when it should change, and you will get two different answers. That is not their fault. It has never been written down. The incident type is currently trying to be everything to everyone: what happened, how serious it was, who was involved, how it ended, and who asked us to attend. A field that carries all of that classifies nothing reliably.

The result is that a single incident can reasonably be categorised several different ways, and in practice, it is:

- There is no guidance on when something is a Marine Incident versus a Vessel Incident, so the same capsize lands in different places on different shifts.
- With no better guidance, a large share of in-water work is generalised to Rescue (In Water), Condition Unknown, and the detail is lost.
- Recovered from Water and Resuscitation overlap with no rule between them. Today we cannot tell whether a resuscitation was a patient we came across on the beach or a person we pulled from the water. Those are profoundly different stories, and our data cannot separate them.
- We cannot distinguish between assisting another agency to do their job and delivering our own service with other agencies alongside. Both look the same in the data.
- There is no rule for when an incident type should be updated, so sometimes it is and sometimes it is not, based on each individual's experience and view of what should happen. When a rescue becomes a drowning, the type is often overwritten, and the rescue disappears from the record. We cannot search for our Major Rescues, because some of them are no longer typed as rescues.
- The same confusion exists between records: there is no clear rule for when something is an incident, a rescue log, or a first aid form, so it is done inconsistently, and our statistics inherit that inconsistency.

Every one of these problems flows from the same root cause: none of these fields has a written definition, so each has drifted into whatever each operator understood it to be.

**What it costs us.** Every season, the EMCaR team pulls incident data for SLSA, for councils, for LSV, and for our own clubs and services. Because the data cannot be trusted at face value, each pull means manual interrogation and cleanup before anyone will stand behind the numbers. The effort is large, it repeats every season, and it caps what we can do: reporting we cannot produce, trends we cannot see, and questions we cannot answer.

## Why now

People have been saying for years that incident categorisation needs to be redone. It has not happened, because it is genuinely complex: 72 types, years of accumulated practice, and interagency dependencies. There is a lot of detail in this pack for the same reason. But the solution underneath it is simple, and once the core idea lands, everything else follows from it.

Two things make this the right moment:

**Our role has changed.** LSV Comms once spent its time signing on every unit. Digital advances in LIMSOC have retired that work. The principal job of LSV Comms now is to get the data right: to capture what actually happened in an incident, accurately and consistently. This proposal is that job.

**We have done this before.** Last season we replaced a rudimentary first aid form that was not fit for purpose. The old form asked a small set of basic questions that often did not match what had happened, and gave members no way to record the details that mattered. The new form asks questions based on what occurred: tick that oxygen was used, and the oxygen questions appear. The result was visibility we had never had. For the first time we could drill into the data and trust what it told us: which first aids are trending, where forms are being filled out incorrectly, and what is actually happening on our beaches. This proposal extends that same transformation from first aid to our entire incident response.

One more thing should be said plainly: this is a change, and change costs effort. But the current structure is already broken. Every season we run it, we accumulate more inconsistent data. Done well, we cannot get worse than we are today. We can only get better.

---

# Part 2: The proposal

## One idea: every value answers exactly one question

The whole model reduces to one principle. Every value attached to an incident answers exactly one question, and no two mechanisms answer the same question. This removes the ambiguity, streamlines the flow for members, and eliminates the duplication that degrades our data today. It simplifies our world: users' lives get easier, and the result gets better.

For the first time, each mechanism gets a written definition:

| Question | Mechanism | Cardinality | Example |
|----------|-----------|-------------|---------|
| What is it, fundamentally | Type (inheritance tree) | one | SAR, Rescue, Person |
| What qualifies or characterises it | Tags (the Incident Labels work, priority 1.8) | many | Resuscitation, Rescue Completed, External Request |
| Where is it in the lifecycle | Agency Status | one at a time | Responding, On Scene, Under Control |
| How did it end | Incident Outcome | one, gated by Type | Resolved, False Alarm, Fatality, Located |
| Assistance provided to one individual | Action Log (proposed merge of first aid form and rescue log, see below) | one per person helped | rescue, resus, fracture, marine sting |
| Part of a bigger event | Event | one | Wye River Floods |
| Free-form situational context | Incident Log | append-only | narrative entries with author and time |
| Free-form summary | Incident Name and Incident Brief | one each | short human-readable identifiers |

**Governing rule.** A value only earns its place as a Type if it changes what the incident fundamentally is. Otherwise it is a Tag, a Status, an Outcome, or Action Log detail.

Two definitions anchor everything else:

**Incident.** A response by Life Saving Victoria members that either:

- Requires a response from multiple lifesaving services, or
- Requires assistance from other emergency services, including all situations where there is a danger to human life, or
- Is otherwise serious or complex such that members would like support, assistance, and visibility from LSV Command.

**Event.** A major occurrence that results in, or has the potential to result in, multiple Incidents. An Event is the vehicle for associating multiple Incidents that share a common cause or context. Not all incidents will require an event association. Example: Wye River Floods.

## The fields around the Type

Before the type tree itself, the supporting fields. Each exists to take a job off the Type, so the Type can do one job well.

### Agency Status: where we are

Captures our overall status as an agency across the life of the incident:

1. Collecting Information
2. Responding
3. On Scene
4. Under Control
5. Returning
6. Finalising
7. Information Only (monitoring, aware but no active response)

Agency Status also carries the advisory-versus-response distinction: Information Only covers the advisory posture, and every other status is a response. This is why the model adopts no priority codes. MPDS surfaces ProQA determinant codes (Delta, Charlie, Bravo, Alpha, Omega), but for lifesaving we are either responding or it is advisory, and the status already says which. A priority field would duplicate information the model already holds.

### Incident Outcome: how it ended

A required selection when closing an incident. Controlled and mutually exclusive, with the options gated by Type:

- A Search surfaces: Located, Fatality, Stood Down.
- A Medical surfaces: Resolved, Referred to Agency, Fatality.
- A Rescue Equipment Activation surfaces the same outcomes as a Rescue, plus False Alarm.

The payoff is searchability. Today, when a rescue ends in a drowning, the type gets overwritten and the rescue vanishes from our statistics. With Outcome as its own field, we keep both truths: it was a Rescue, and it ended in a Fatality. We can finally search on each independently.

### Tags: what characterised it

Tags characterise. They never classify. An incident carries as many as apply. Draft groups:

**Care and clinical (form triggers).** Resuscitation, Member Injury, Penthrane Administered, Major First Aid, Oxygen Administered (each requiring an Action Log entry), and Rescue Completed (requiring the rescue detail, including method such as Heli rescue technique, which must flow back to the incident record: a platform requirement).

**Operational context.** External Request (a request originating outside LSV, distinct from the External Agency > Request for Assistance Type), Off-duty response, Multi-agency, Extrication, Mass Rescue (a scale tag on a Rescue or SAR).

**Vessel Incident modifiers.** Injury / No Injury.

**Dangerous Animal modifiers.** Confirmed / Reported, and Confirmation source (Lifeguard, Aerial, Member of public, External agency).

The full tag taxonomy is being drafted with the Incident Labels project (priority 1.8); the two are one effort.

### Incident Log, Name, and Brief

The Incident Log is the append-only narrative: timestamped entries with an author, carrying the situational context that does not belong in structured fields. Incident Name and Incident Brief remain the short human-readable identifiers.

## A new kind of Type

With every other question answered by a purpose-built field, the Type is free to answer just one: **what is the nature of the situation we are responding to?** The Type reflects the primary driver of the response, not everything that happens during it. A rescue followed by first aid is still a Rescue. A member of the public presenting on the beach with a major first aid is a Medical incident.

The structural change is to replace the current flat category-and-type list with an inheritance tree. A type can be the parent of another type, so classification becomes a walk from general to specific, and the operator is guided to a single correct answer instead of choosing from a list of 72. Fewer types overall, one clear home for every situation, and no scenario where two options are equally valid.

## Type states and guided questions

Two mechanisms make the tree work in practice.

**Type states.** Every node in the tree carries a state that governs when it can be used:

| State | Can open as this? | Can close as this? | Purpose |
|-------|-------------------|--------------------|---------|
| **Abstract** | No | No | Grouping node only. Structure and reporting, not selection. |
| **Not Final** | Yes | No | Can be opened while the specific nature is unknown. Must be refined to a Final child before closure. |
| **Final** | Yes | Yes | Fully specific. Terminal in the tree. |

For example, Medical is Not Final: an incident can be opened as Medical while the presenting problem is still being assessed, but before closure it must be refined to Chest Pain, Breathing Problems, and so on. Search and Rescue is Abstract: a bare SAR cannot be opened, one of its children must be selected. Chest Pain is Final.

This is also what retires the catch-all types (Other Incident, Other Medical, Other Vessel Incident). Instead of dumping the unknown into an "Other" bucket that tells us nothing, operators open at the most specific node they know, and refine before closure. Open wide, close narrow.

**Guided questions.** A Type may carry key questions, in the style of ProQA (the scripted question flow used by MPDS dispatch systems). Each answer does one of two things: drills to a child Type, or sets a controlled Tag. No per-incident custom fields are created; the questions populate the existing primitives. Questions are centrally defined per Type, and an answer never maps to free text that fragments data. A deliberately small set of true structured fields is kept only where the value is quantitative and reporting-critical (for example, number of people involved). Everything else defaults to Tags.

Specificity comes from the tree walk and the questions, not from a long type list.

## The types

With the concepts in place, the tree itself:

- **Search And Rescue** [Abstract]
    - **Search** [Abstract]
        - Person [Not Final]
            - Land [Final]
            - Water [Final]
        - Vessel [Final]
    - **Rescue** [Abstract]
        - Person [Not Final]
            - Land [Final]
            - Water [Final]
        - Vessel [Final]
    - **Emergency** [Abstract]
        - Rescue Equipment Activation [Final]
        - Duress Activation [Final]
        - Flare Sighting [Final]
- **Welfare Check** [placement and state to be confirmed, see Part 4]
- **Medical** [Not Final]
    - MPDS-aligned children, see the Medical branch below.
- **External Agency** [Abstract]
    - Tasking [Final]
    - Request for Assistance [Final]
- **Marine Incident** [Abstract]
    - **Vessel Incident** [Abstract]
        - Assist [Final]
        - Report [Final]
    - **Dangerous Animal** [Abstract]
        - Shark [Final]
        - Other [Final]
- **Advisory Information** [Abstract]
    - Dangerous Conditions [Final]
    - Equipment Fault [Final]

## The rules that keep the data consistent

Four rules govern classification. Each one closes a specific gap that corrupts our data today.

### Rule 1: The Type is what we responded to

- The Type is updated only when new information clarifies that the initial classification was incorrect.
- The Type is never updated because the incident evolved.
- Evolution is captured in the Agency Status, the Incident Outcome, Tags, and the Incident Log.

This is the rule that fixes the disappearing Major Rescue. The rescue that becomes a drowning stays a Rescue, with Outcome: Fatality. It aligns with Ambulance Victoria practice, which does not recategorise unless the incident was misreported. And because the rule is written down, "sometimes updated, sometimes not" ends: no more individual judgment calls producing inconsistent records.

### Rule 2: One Type per incident

The Type captures the primary operational driver. Where two drivers genuinely co-occur, precedence selects the Type:

1. Search and Rescue or Rescue (a save wins)
2. Marine Incident
3. Medical
4. Advisory Information

Supporting principles: human first, vessel second (where a situation involves both people and a vessel, the Type follows the people); clinical detail always rides in the Action Log, never as a competing Type; and multiple separate responses to one situation group under an Event, they are not merged into one incident.

**Worked scenarios.**

1. **Rescue then major medical.** Swimmer pulled from a rip, arrests on the beach. Type is Rescue. Resuscitation rides as a Tag (Action Log required) and in the Action Log detail.
2. **Vessel incident producing a rescue.** Capsized vessel, people retrieved. Type is Rescue. Human first, vessel second. The vessel dimension is Tags and log.
3. **Medical during an External Agency Tasking.** Severity decides. A severe injury becomes its own linked incident. A minor one stays on the Tasking incident with a Member Injury Tag.
4. **Activation that becomes a rescue.** Stays one incident, typed as the activation. See Rule 4.

### Rule 3: Our incident or theirs

Whether something is a Tasking or our own incident is determined by our response. Are we delivering our services independently (including as part of an interagency response)? Then we open an incident of the appropriate type. Are we assisting another agency to perform their duties? Then it is External Agency > Tasking. This closes today's gap where the two are indistinguishable in the data.

**Worked example.** AV asks us to help carry their patient off the beach. We are a resource on AV's job: External Agency > Tasking, with tags and log notes as required. If instead we are managing the patient and called AV, it is Medical, with AV listed in responding services.

Extrication is an action, so it is a Tag, never a Type. This retires Assist Extrication as a Type.

### Rule 4: Activations keep their Type

When a Rescue Equipment Activation or Duress Activation leads to a real rescue, the incident stays as the activation Type it was opened as. One incident, no reclassification, no second incident. The rescue that follows is carried in Agency Status, Tags, Incident Outcome, and the log.

## The Action Log

*New in v0.8. Proposed here as a concept; detail to follow as its own piece of work.*

Today we run two per-person records, the first aid form and the rescue log, with no clear rule for when each applies. A person pulled from the water and treated on the beach might generate one, both, or neither, depending on who is filling it out. Members enter the same person's details twice when both apply. The inconsistency flows straight into our rescue and first aid statistics.

The proposal: merge them into one **Action Log**, defined as the assistance we provide to one individual. That assistance may be a rescue, a first aid, or both. The expectation becomes simple enough to say in one sentence: **one Action Log for each person we help, every time.** The person's details are entered once. Where the situation meets the criteria for an incident, the Action Logs are linked to that incident, exactly as first aid records link today.

This gives the guided-questions machinery a natural home on the per-person record too: the adaptive first aid form we already built becomes a section of the Action Log, appearing when care was provided, alongside rescue detail that appears when a rescue was performed.

Platform implications are noted in Annex C. This proposal supersedes the earlier First Aid Log (FAL) terminology decision, noted in the Decision Log.

## What this makes possible

Consistent, well-defined data is not the end goal. It is the foundation.

- **Backwards compatibility comes built in.** Every one of the 72 current types maps to exactly one home in the new model: a Type, a Tag, an Outcome, a Status, or a linked-record concept. Nothing is lost, and historical data stays comparable. The full map is Annex A.
- **Guided questions get smarter over time.** Centrally governed question flows can grow per Type without adding types or fields.
- **AI-enabled features become possible.** Structured, predictable data is the prerequisite for the features we want next: guided incident creation, quality checks at point of entry, automated summaries.
- **Expectations can rise naturally.** With clear definitions and a simpler flow, we can ask more of our members, because for the first time the system makes the right way the easy way.

**Operators** get a guided path instead of a 72-item list, and a written definition for every field. The system asks the questions; the operator answers what they know. Faster incident creation, less second-guessing, and no more choosing between two equally defensible types at 2am.

**Duty officers and command** get a consistent common operating picture. The same situation looks the same regardless of who entered it or which shift entered it. Status, type, and outcome each mean one thing, so the picture reads at a glance.

That reliability compounds into everything the data touches: how we structure our services, how we support our members, and how we make the case for funding.

# Annex C: Platform dev notes

Design constraints the platform must support.

**Required documentation rules.**

- Set required documents against an Incident Type. Inputs can include People (for example, patient count).
- Set required documents against Incident Tags.
- Distinguish between "form submission required" and "specific section within a form required".

**Tag scoping.**

- Constrain Tags to specific Incident Types by inclusion or exclusion. A Tag that only makes sense for Medical should not appear on a Marine Incident.

**Type states, platform behaviour.**

- Types are Abstract, Not Final, or Final. See Part 2, Type states.
- Abstract Types cannot be selected on open or close.
- Not Final Types can be opened but not closed. The user is prompted to refine before finalising.
- Final Types can be opened and closed.

**Action Log (proposed).**

- A single per-person record replacing the first aid form and rescue log. One Action Log per individual assisted.
- Sections appear conditionally: care sections when treatment was provided (the adaptive first aid form becomes a section), rescue detail when a rescue was performed (method, including Heli technique, flowing back to the incident record).
- Action Logs link to an incident when the incident criteria are met, as first aid records link today.
- Existing form-trigger Tags (Resuscitation, Member Injury, Penthrane Administered, Major First Aid, Oxygen Administered, Rescue Completed) become Action Log requirements.

People have been saying for years that incident categorisation needs to be redone. It has not happened, because it is genuinely complex: 72 types, years of accumulated practice, and interagency dependencies. There is a lot of detail in this pack for the same reason. But the solution underneath it is simple, and once the core idea lands, everything else follows from it.

Two things make this the right moment:

**Our role has changed.** LSV Comms once spent its time signing on every unit. Digital advances in LIMSOC have retired that work. The principal job of LSV Comms now is to get the data right: to capture what actually happened in an incident, accurately and consistently. This proposal is that job.

**We have done this before.** Last season we replaced a rudimentary first aid form that was not fit for purpose. The old form asked a small set of basic questions that often did not match what had happened, and gave members no way to record the details that mattered. The new form asks questions based on what occurred: tick that oxygen was used, and the oxygen questions appear. The result was visibility we had never had. For the first time we could drill into the data and trust what it told us: which first aids are trending, where forms are being filled out incorrectly, and what is actually happening on our beaches. This proposal extends that same transformation from first aid to our entire incident response.

One more thing should be said plainly: this is a change, and change costs effort. But the current structure is already broken. Every season we run it, we accumulate more inconsistent data. Done well, we cannot get worse than we are today. We can only get better.

input.old_string: The current model provides no written definition of what an incident type represents or when it should be updated. A field that carries all of these dimensions cannot classify any of them reliably, and each operator's interpretation of it necessarily differs.

input.old_string: **The approach is proven.** Last season the first aid form was rebuilt from a rudimentary form that was not fit for purpose. For the first time the data could be interrogated with confidence: which first aid presentations are trending, where forms are completed incorrectly, and what is occurring on our beaches. This proposal applies the same transformation to the incident record.
